changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from CV Austere & Disaster Medicine Part One: scene zones, identification tools, responder training tiers, decontamination flow, and the pulmonary-irritant / asphyxiant / nerve-agent toxidromes.

summary: The operating picture for a chemical release: three zones, four responder tiers, a decontamination corridor that protects everyone downstream of it, and the three toxidrome families a medical provider actually has to tell apart — irritant gas, asphyxiant, and cholinergic.
whyThisMatters: A contaminated patient who reaches your resus bay undecontaminated turns one casualty into a contaminated department. The scene structure and decon corridor exist to stop that, and they only work if the medical team understands where its boundary is. On the clinical side, the agent that kills late — phosgene, with pulmonary edema up to 48 hours out — looks tolerable at first contact, so recognition and a disposition rule matter more than any antidote.
clinicalTakeaway: Medical providers work in the cold zone, upwind and uphill; only decontaminated patients cross into it, and clothing removal alone clears most contamination. Sort the exposure into one of three toxidromes: water-soluble irritants (chlorine, ammonia) announce themselves and are supportive-care only; phosgene is deceptively mild early — observe any exposure for the full 48-hour delayed-edema window; chemical asphyxiants (cyanide, CO, H2S) impair oxygen use at the cell and cyanide has a specific antidote (hydroxocobalamin ± sodium thiosulfate). Copious secretions, miosis, and seizures mark a cholinergic/nerve-agent exposure — atropine plus pralidoxime.

body.text: Foundational scene reference. The cholinergic/nerve-agent, vesicant, and radiological sections are previews here — full antidote protocols and agent-specific decontamination belong in dedicated expansions.

rows: Contaminated area immediately around the source
Hazmat-technician training + appropriate PPE only. Medical providers without this do not enter.
Decontamination corridor between hot and cold zones
Operations-level responders — defensive actions and emergency decon
Clean area upwind and uphill of the release
Command, triage, and stabilized patient care. Only decontaminated patients enter.

items: Identification tools: DOT placards (diamond, hazard class + 4-digit UN ID number); NFPA 704 fixed-facility placards (red = flammability, blue = health, yellow = reactivity, white = special hazard); shipping documents; the Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG).
Position the cold zone upwind and uphill of the release — a wind shift is a scene-safety event.

rows: Recognize a release, isolate the area, deny entry, notify authority. No hands-on mitigation.
Defensive actions only — exclusion zones, basic containment, emergency decontamination. Does not approach the source.
Offensive, hands-on actions to stop the release, including hot-zone entry for product control and confinement.
The regulatory standard underlying these tiers for emergency response and waste-site operations.

items: Emergency decon: rapid gross decontamination (copious water irrigation, clothing removal) in the warm zone for severely symptomatic patients before formal technical decon is feasible.
Technical decon: structured multi-step process for less acute exposures, ideally capturing runoff.
Clothing removal alone removes the majority of contamination in most exposures — double-bag clothing and personal items separately.
Self-decontamination: ambulatory patients can be directed through self-decon with clear pictorial, multilingual instructions, preserving responder capacity for non-ambulatory casualties.
Cold-zone arrival: only decontaminated patients move forward. This boundary is what protects the rest of the medical response from secondary contamination.

body.text: Spans industrial chemicals (chlorine, ammonia) and historical warfare agents (phosgene). Water solubility sets the clinical signature: highly soluble agents announce themselves at once; poorly soluble agents do not.

rows: Immediate, intense mucous-membrane and upper-airway irritation; pungent odor even at low concentration — the chemical announces itself
Mild, deceptively tolerable initial irritation; severe pulmonary edema delayed up to 48 hours after exposure

body.text: No antidote exists for phosgene or chlorine — treatment is entirely supportive (remove from exposure, oxygen, nebulized bronchodilators, corticosteroids, lung-protective ventilation if ARDS develops). Any phosgene-exposed patient needs observation for the full delayed-edema window even if asymptomatic at presentation — early discharge can miss the lethal phase.

rows: Displace oxygen from the breathing environment; no independent toxicity
Impair oxygen utilization at the cellular level even with adequate ambient oxygen

items: Management: remove from the environment immediately, give 100% oxygen.
Cyanide has specific antidotes — hydroxocobalamin, sodium thiosulfate — where chemical asphyxiation is confirmed or strongly suspected.

body.text: Organophosphate pesticides and military nerve agents (sarin, VX) share one mechanism: acetylcholinesterase inhibition, producing a cholinergic toxidrome distinct from irritant-gas exposure. Full dosing and decontamination specifics are reserved for a dedicated expansion.

items: Quick recognition — SLUDGE / DUMBELS: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis; and defecation, urination, miosis, bradycardia/bronchorrhea, emesis, lacrimation, salivation.
Distinguishing feature: miosis, copious secretions, and seizures separate this toxidrome from the irritant-gas pattern.
First-line antidote: atropine (muscarinic blockade) plus pralidoxime (reactivates acetylcholinesterase if given before aging).
